nodes.title: UPDATES
nodes.body: April 14, 1989.  Thomas Czapla; NOAA SEA Division

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Bay Scallop
Scientific Name: Argopecten irradians
Other Common Names: Atlantic Bay scallop.

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Mollusca
Class: Bivalvia
Order: Ostreoida
Family: Pectinidae

nodes.title: Subspecific Names
nodes.body:
Argopecten irradians consists of three subspecies: A. i. irradians, ranging from Cape Cod to New Jersey; A. i. concentricus, New Jersey to the Chandeleur Islands, east of the Mississippi River; and A. i. amplicostatus, Galveston Bay to the Laguna Madre, Texas (208).


Note: Subclass	Pteriomorphia (Beurlen, 1944)

nodes.title: Value
nodes.body:
Commercial: There is no apparent commercial fishery for this species in the Texas area because of their low densities.

Recreational: They are taken by the public for food; however their scarcity makes the trouble hardly worth it.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
0verall: Ranges along the western Atlantic from Cape Cod to the Laguna Madre in the Gulf of Mexico.

Within Study Area: More abundant in the south bays of Texas were the salinities are generally higher. The subspecies Argopectin irradians amplicostatus ranges from central Texas to Tuxapan, Veracruz, Mexico (14).

Movements and Migrations
Bay Scallop juveniles and adults have swimming abilities apparently serving to maintain position in grassbeds and avoid competitors and predators (558 771).

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs are demersal.
Larvae are pelagic.
Juveniles attach to rocks by byssus.
Adults are epifaunal and gregarious.

nodes.title: Habitat
nodes.body:
Type: All life stages are estuarine, and marine in nearshore waters. Recorded at depths from 0-10 m and a maximum of 18 m; most abundant in waters from 0.3-0.6 m at low tide (433 619 723 556 208 219).

Substrate: Found over silt and hard sand usually in association with sea grasses and other submerged macrophytes.

nodes.title: Physical/chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature: Eggs and larvae are stenothermal with 15-20 C required for early development, optimal embryonic development at 20-25 and best larval growth at 25-30 C (720). Juveniles and adults are eurythermal, able to tolerate subfreezing temperatures for short periods (433). Wright et al. (776) found larvae subjected to temperatures below the spawning temperature experienced a cold-shock which resulted in higher mortalities.

Salinity: Eggs and larvae are polyhaline, optimal around 22.5 ppt (100). Larvae develop 20-35 ppt with optimum at 25 (720); not found below 22 ppt. Juveniles and adults are euryhaline tolerating very low salinities but show signs of stress when below 16 ppt (621 191).

Turbidity: Turbidities greater than 500 ppm may interfere with normal growth and reproduction (208).

Growth and Development
Egg: Fertilized eggs rapidly develop to trochophore larvae by about 24 h.

nodes.title: Reproduction
nodes.body:
Repro Mode: Hermaphroditic, usually protandrous (556); semelparous. Fertilization is external, in the water column or on the bottom.

Mating and Spawning: Spawning is temperature related, occurring in estuaries and nearshore at various times throughout the range. In the northeast spawning is triggered by increasing temperatures (717); while south from North Carolina spawning is triggered by decreasing temperatures (29). In Florida, spawning begins with the decline in summer temperatures, August to October (619 29).

Reproductive Capacity: Kraeuter et a1 (389) reported fecundity of 100,000 to 1,000,000 eggs per female.  Bricelj et a1 (1987) reported fecundities ten to twenty times greater.

Growth and Development
Egg: Fertilized eggs rapidly develop to trochophore larvae by about 24 h.

Larvae: Trochophore to straight-hinged larvae occurs in about 24 h (267 620). At about 10-12 days the larva (prodissoconch) settles to the bottom and attaches itself to the substrate by byssus threads. The juvenile stage is reached after larval development in about 29 days from fertilization (620). Loosanoff and Davis (418) reported larval growth rate to be greater than 10 um a day.

Juvenile: Growth is dependent on temperature and food availability. During winter minimal growth occurs. Rates of 3.8-8.0 mm/mo have been determined.

Adult: Maturity is reached by the end of the first year; a function of age and not size. Adult sizes range from 60-70 mm with a reported maximum of 90 mm. Life expectancy is 12-26 months, usually less than two years.

Food and Feeding
Scallops filter feed primarily on phytoplankton, but also consume zooplankton, suspended benthic particles, bacteria, detritus, organic matter, gametes from other species and algae spores. Chipman (114) determined that young scallops filter at a rate of 3 l/h, which increases as they grow reaching an average of 15 l/h, and a maximum of 25.4 l/h. Intensity of feeding increases with temperature.

Ecological Interactions and Notes
